segments.text: This is a DIY RC sim-racing controller: a receiver adapter, a handful of firmware, a custom case I modelled myself, and then a rather brave track test.
Here it is on track — the RC controller in one hand while I drive, and that receiver signal is what my little adapter turns into an ordinary USB joystick.
Let us look at the firmware, because the whole trick is only a handful of lines. It is an Arduino sketch called rc controller.
First it pulls in Joystick dot h, a library that turns the board into a standard USB game controller, so the PC needs no special driver.
Then it names the two inputs: throttle on digital pin two, and steering on digital pin three.
In setup, both pins are set as inputs, and Joystick dot begin hands the controller over to the operating system.
The clever part is the axis ranges: set X axis range from nineteen hundred down to ten fifty, and the Y axis the other way round.
An RC receiver sends a pulse between roughly one and two milliseconds, and the ends come in reversed — so the firmware deliberately flips them back into the right direction.
The main loop then does the real work. pulse in measures the length of the pulse arriving on each pin, and that length is the stick position.
Steering goes to the X axis and throttle to the Y axis, so the transmitter moves the joystick. And that is the entire adapter.
The board needed a home, so I modelled a case in 3table, the CAD editor I built myself.
Starting from a blank grid, I shaped a long grey shell around the board — snap-fit tabs and a power switch up front.
Inside there are ribs, threaded mounting posts and slots that hold the board exactly where it needs to sit.
Then came the track test. Full disclosure: I was filming with one hand and steering with the other, so the driving is, frankly, brave. But the controller worked, and that is the whole point.
A receiver adapter, a few dozen lines of firmware, a case modelled in 3table, and one very sketchy lap.
